# The Opportunity Feed


[Chelsey Sassine](https://medium.com/@chelseysassine?source=post_page---byline--88b3818cbc3a------------------------------------------)


5 min read


·


2 hours ago

*Why good engineering can still be bad business*


Press enter or click to view image in full size


The refinery I worked at was an opportunity refiner. We made our money buying whatever the market was selling at a discount and figuring out how to run it.


One day the economics group found a cheap, partly refined feed that would let us push more through one of our gasoline units. Feeds like that are called opportunity feeds, and they tend to be too good to be true. Operations objected. We ran it anyway, and it started fouling the unit almost immediately.


So I put pencil to paper and worked out how fast the deposits were building. At that rate, we’d have to shut the unit down to clean it within months, so I recommended we stop. Everyone agreed the economics model had missed the hidden cost, and the economics team took my findings back to fix it.


I was proud of that. Then the VP of Operations pulled me aside and said, “You’re a really good engineer, but you’ll be a great engineer when you understand that we’re a business.”


I had been optimizing the unit. The business needed me to optimize the margin.


The opportunity feed wasn’t the only thing going into the unit. At a lower rate, the regular feed diluted the compound that caused the deposits, so they formed less often. The fouling slowed down more than the feed rate did, and the best margin came from cutting the feed back, not cutting it out.


Most software teams have been optimizing the unit for years. Engineers sit far enough from the economics that a clean codebase starts to look like the goal. Reading every line to keep the fouling out starts to look like the job. But if you run the margin math on a software team today, it says the opposite of what the refinery found — maximize throughput.


## Do the math


Take a team of five engineers at $100,000 each. Benefits and overhead push the real cost higher, but the low number is enough. That’s $500,000 a year, or about $42,000 a month for the team. They’re building a feature that takes three months, a $125,000 investment. Most teams won’t approve that unless it’s expected to pay for itself within a year of release, so it needs to earn at least $10,400 a month once it ships.


The feature is only live for nine months of its first year, so it earns about $94,000. By the end of the year, it still hasn’t paid for itself. Now give the team AI and clear the bottlenecks around it, and the same feature takes one month. It costs about $42,000 and earns about $115,000. Get it down to a week, and it costs about $10,000 and earns about $123,000. The cost fell by more than 90 percent, and the feature earned more because it went live sooner.


The bigger gain is what the team does with the time it got back. Here’s the same team shipping one feature after another for a year, each one earning about $10,400 a month.


Press enter or click to view image in full size


The team costs $500,000 a year in every row. At a quarterly pace, it earns back less than half its cost in the first year. At a monthly pace, it comes out ahead. At a weekly pace, it returns more than six times its cost. Throughput compounds. Every feature that ships early earns money while the next one is being built.


Right now, for most software teams, the margin is in throughput, and it isn’t close. That’s why this series started with finding the bottleneck.


## When throughput runs out


The refinery got a different answer from the same math because it was a mature process. A unit that has run for decades has had its bottlenecks worked over and over. Every fix bought less than the one before, until the unit ran at its limit and there was little throughput left to win.


When throughput is maxed out, margin comes from two other levers. **Yield** is how much of what goes in comes out as something you can sell. **Efficiency** is what each unit of product costs to make.


The opportunity feed was a throughput and efficiency play, which is why it looked so good on paper. It cost less than making the same thing from crude, and it filled space the crude couldn’t at the time. At full rate, though, it fouled the unit fast enough to limit the whole refinery’s throughput, which would wipe out the savings. Cutting the feed back gave up a little throughput to keep most of the efficiency, and that’s where the margin peaked.


Software will get there. As the bottlenecks fall, the assumptions behind the throughput math start to break. The team runs out of ideas that pay for themselves in a year. Changes made in a hurry leave shortcuts behind, and tech debt starts fouling the system.


That’s when the other two levers start to matter. Yield becomes the share of changes that land right the first time instead of coming back as rework. Efficiency becomes what each change costs in engineer time, tokens, and compute. Switching to a cheaper model or a leaner architecture is an efficiency play, just like the opportunity feed, and it can cost you yield or throughput the same way.


An agent setup that ships twice the changes with three times the rework might be your most profitable option, or it might not. But the most profitable system is rarely the perfect one. A refinery at 85 percent yield beats one at 99 percent if it runs twice the throughput.


## Optimize the margin


I’d made plenty of economic calls before, but every one of them protected the unit. I’d never had to let it foul on purpose. That conversation stuck, and I carried it with me into software.


A good engineer optimizes the system. A great engineer optimizes the margin. Pulling one lever is easy. The real work starts when throughput, yield, and efficiency pull against each other, and the only way through is to do the math.
